source_title: How rich is Jerry Jones? Breaking down the Cowboys owner's net worth, business empire and NFL fortune - The Times of India
source_excerpt: Jerry Jones is worth somewhere between $13 billion and $23 billion, depending on who is counting. Forbes put him and his family at $20.3 billion on its 2026 world list, and its latest report lists him at $23.2 billion. The Dallas Cowboys, which he bought for $140 million in 1989, are now valued at a record $17 billion. That gap between estimates shows how hard it is to price a man whose biggest asset has never been for sale. Here is what he owns, how he built it and which numbers deserve trust.How rich is Jerry Jones right now?Pick a source and you get a different answer. On the Forbes world list, Jones and his family rank No. 128, up from $16.6 billion in 2025. The live figure has since climbed, and it makes him No. 9 on Forbes' list of the richest U.S. sports team owners. Celebrity Net Worth still carries $13 billion. That number looks dated, because it matches what Forbes said the Cowboys alone were worth last year.Why such a spread? Nobody can read Jones's bank statements. He owns a private team, private land and private energy investments, so every outlet has to estimate. Some update when the team's value jumps. Others lag behind.Treat all of them as informed guesses. The safest reading is that Jones sits above $20 billion on the best-sourced tracker, and that the franchise drives most of it. All figures here are estimates as of late October 2026.From a $140 million purchase to a $17 billion teamJones bought the club from Bum Bright in 1989. The first season ended 1-15. He had just fired Tom Landry, the only head coach the franchise had ever known, and taken over football decisions himself. Dallas was not happy. Then things flipped fast. Jimmy Johnson, his old Arkansas teammate, built a roster that won Super Bowls XXVII and XXVIII, and Barry Switzer added XXX after the 1995 season.The Johnson partnership broke apart in 1994 over credit and control. Years later, asked why Johnson still has no spot in the team's Ring of Honor, Jones said: "Disloyalty â¦ I couldn't handle the disloyalty." It is a revealing line. It shows how personal this business has always been for him.The titles stopped after that January 1996 win. The money did not. Forbes ranked the Cowboys first for the 20th straight year, ahead of the Rams at $13.5 billion, the Giants at $12 billion and the Patriots at $10.6 billion. Dallas generated nearly $1.28 billion in revenue last season, slightly more than Real Madrid, and an estimated $677 million in operating income, $342 million ahead of the next-best NFL team.Pause on that. A team that has not won a Super Bowl in three decades is still the most profitable operation in sports. Winning helps, but ownership at this level sells attention, and Dallas has more of it than anyone. Seattle's $9.6 billion sale to Vinod Khosla shows how fast the whole league is rising, yet the Cowboys still sit far above it.The business machine around the starJones did not just hold the asset and wait. Early in his tenure he pushed for Fox to become a major NFL television partner while older networks wanted to pay less. That move is credited with lifting league TV revenue, and every owner benefits from a bigger pot, Dallas included.Then came buildings. AT&T Stadium, a billion-dollar venue in Arlington, turned game days into an events business. In 2008 he teamed with Yankee Global Enterprises to start Legends Hospitality, which runs food, drink, merchandise and operations at venues such as Cowboys Stadium.Land is the quieter play. His real estate firm, Blue Star Land, paid $38 million in 2018 for a 200-acre site that became Star Business Park. It added another 60 acres in 2019. Part of that ground is planned for a 400,000-square-foot merchandise and distribution center for the team.Each piece feeds the next. The stadium draws crowds, Legends serves them, and the land captures what grows around it. That is why his wealth is not simply a bet on the scoreboard.Where the rest of his money comes fromJones was a deal maker long before he owned a team. In the 1960s he borrowed $1 million from the Teamsters to open Shakey's Pizza restaurants in Missouri. The venture failed. He then worked at his father's insurance firm, returned to Arkansas for a business master's degree in 1970 and launched Jones Oil and Land Lease. Forbes says he earned his first million in 1970s oil investments, and he still backs drilling plus retail and residential real estate around Dallas. Wealth trackers also link him to Comstock Resources, a natural gas producer.Some of it is spent in plain sight. Forbes reported a cost of about $250 million for his 357-foot superyacht, though other coverage puts it nearer $225 million. His Highland Park home in Dallas is valued around $20 million.The family business is also the family. Stephen is chief operating officer and handles player personnel. Charlotte oversees charities and special events. Jerry Jr. leads sales and marketing. Jones gave all three limited partnership interests in the early 1990s, so the succession plan has been moving for decades.At 84, Jones still holds the owner, president and general manager roles.
